analysis.one_liner: Keeps offshore oil and gas leasing open under an older, broader federal plan.
analysis.headline: A single-sponsor bill with zero cosponsors never got a committee hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the Obama administration's five-year plan for leasing offshore federal waters for oil and gas drilling and instead kept the older, broader leasing plan in force through 2020. It would have also declared, by law, that the environmental review for that older plan was already complete, so no new review would be required. A few named lease sales would have been left out. The bill never moved after being sent to the Senate energy committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that want access to offshore federal tracts: the bill would have kept more areas available for lease sales than the administration's plan allowed, and removed the need for a fresh environmental review. Energy consumers could see a small, indirect benefit from additional domestic supply over time.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would declare the older Draft Proposed 2010-2015 leasing program to be the final program for fiscal years 2015 through 2020, keeping leasing operating under that broader plan instead of the administration's more limited 2012-2017 program [S2][S3].

It would deem the required environmental impact statement under the National Environmental Policy Act to have already been issued, so the leasing plan could go forward without a new environmental review [S2][S3].

It specifies that the change would not touch the existing drilling restrictions in the eastern Gulf of Mexico under a 2006 law, and would exclude three named lease sales (214, 232, and 239) from the final program [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities whose economies depend on fishing and tourism would bear the added risk of offshore spills, and the public would lose the environmental review process the bill would bypass. Taxpayers also would not capture more of the value of publicly owned offshore resources beyond what existing lease terms provide.

drawbacks.text: The bill would legislate that the environmental review required by the National Environmental Policy Act is already done, short-circuiting a public process for weighing drilling risks before more offshore areas are offered [S2][S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the tradeoff: more offshore leasing can expand domestic energy supply and lease revenue, but it raises the risk of spills that fall hardest on coastal fishing and tourism economies, which is why the administration's plan had limited where drilling could occur.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs mostly to oil and gas companies seeking access to offshore tracts, and any benefit to consumers from added supply would be indirect and slow. The cost falls on coastal communities exposed to spill risk and on the public's environmental review process. The bill is a one-sponsor measure with no cosponsors and no committee action, so it never received any scrutiny beyond introduction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on its first day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter of Louisiana introduced the bill on January 7, 2015, the opening day of the 114th Congress [S1][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the administration's more limited offshore leasing plan stayed in effect and no new offshore areas were opened without a fresh environmental review. Coastal communities avoided the added spill risk the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities; no new offshore access

for.name: David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no senator cosponsored it [S1][S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — and it expired with the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no party bloc ever took a position on it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have kept a broader set of offshore areas available for lease sales and waived the need for a new environmental review, expanding drilling access for companies that hold or seek federal offshore leases. More supply could modestly lower energy costs, but the main gain is lease access for the industry itself [S2][S3].

Expanded offshore drilling raises the risk of spills that shut down fisheries and deter beach visitors, and those losses land on local fishing and tourism economies. These businesses' interests in this bill ran against expanded leasing [S3].
